claims.evidence: Lab Tests Online UK: routine testing not recommended for everyone; NHS guidelines advise against testing people with no symptoms who are not at risk.
The test measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 25(OH)D.
Most people make enough vitamin D from sunlight on the skin in spring and summer.
'Levels drop' not stated; sources say the sun is too low for skin to make vitamin D from about October to early March.
claims.newSentence: In the UK, the sun is too low in the sky for the skin to make vitamin D from about October to early March.

claims.evidence: Routine testing not recommended for asymptomatic people.
Doctor may order the test for bone pain or softness in adults and muscle pain or weakness with no obvious cause.
Abnormal calcium, phosphate or parathyroid hormone and known bone disease needing correction before treatment were seen; kidney disease and malabsorption not seen as triggers.
claims.newSentence: It is also considered after abnormal calcium, phosphate or parathyroid hormone results, and before some bone treatments.

claims.evidence: UK prescribing guideline: asymptomatic higher-risk people need no routine testing but should be advised on maintenance supplementation.
Dark skin, little or no sun exposure, and age 65 and over named as higher risk.
Rickets in children seen; 'bone deformities' wording not returned.
claims.newSentence: A lack of vitamin D can cause rickets in children.

claims.evidence: Osteomalacia in adults brings bone pain and tenderness.
Tiredness and aches seen but not attributed to a medical director.
claims.newSentence: Some people notice tiredness or general aches and pains, which are easy to put down to other causes.

claims.evidence: Severe, long-term deficiency can soften bones.
Bands came from Lab Tests Online UK, not an NHS trust.
claims.newSentence: Lab Tests Online UK describes results as deficient, possibly inadequate for some people, or sufficient for almost everyone.

claims.evidence: One guideline: for the middle band treatment may be appropriate in some patients; symptom-driven wording not seen.
claims.newSentence: In the middle band, one NHS guideline says treatment may be appropriate for some patients.

claims.evidence: Cut-offs vary between labs; read the result against the reference range on the lab report.
'Usually set by a clinician' not stated; LTO says the doctor interprets the result with symptoms, bone health and risk factors.
claims.newSentence: A doctor interprets the result in the context of symptoms, bone health and any risk factors.

claims.evidence: UK public health guidance (PHE/NICE statement) advises considering a supplement in autumn and winter; NHS England attribution not seen.
claims.newSentence: UK public health guidance advises that everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.

claims.evidence: Scottish Government: everyone aged 5 and over should consider a daily supplement, especially October to March (NHS inform says over one year).
Higher-risk groups advised all year; includes pregnant and breastfeeding women, under-5s, people with little sun exposure.
African, African-Caribbean and South Asian origin named as year-round risk group in Scotland; NICE similar.
Excess intake can be toxic with high blood calcium; attribution to NHS page not seen.
claims.newSentence: Clinical guidance warns that very high doses of vitamin D can be toxic and raise blood calcium.

claims.evidence: Local NHS guidance: buy over the counter for prevention, prescribe for diagnosed deficiency; 'NHS England moved away' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Local NHS guidance generally says supplements for prevention should be bought over the counter, with prescribing kept for diagnosed deficiency.

claims.evidence: Sunlight on skin in spring and summer is how most people make enough.
Oily fish, egg yolks, fortified foods not confirmed; sources say few foods contain much vitamin D.
claims.newSentence: Few foods contain much vitamin D, so food alone is usually not enough.

claims.evidence: Many people have no symptoms.
Tiredness and general aches and pains noted by some people.
Weak/soft/deformed wording not returned. Rickets and osteomalacia described as best understood consequences.
claims.newSentence: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults are described as the best understood consequences of vitamin D deficiency.

claims.evidence: 'Rickets more common' not returned; dark skin and covering the body named as risk factors for deficiency.
claims.newSentence: Darker skin and covering most of the body with clothing are recognised risk factors for vitamin D deficiency.

claims.evidence: Premature/breastfed babies not seen. LTO: low levels reflect limited sun, low intake or poor absorption.
claims.newSentence: Low levels can reflect limited sun exposure, low dietary intake or a problem absorbing vitamin D from the gut.

claims.evidence: Not routinely tested without symptoms.
Malabsorption and kidney disease as triggers not seen; abnormal calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, bone pain, muscle weakness seen.
claims.newSentence: Testing is considered for bone pain, muscle weakness, or abnormal calcium, phosphate or parathyroid hormone results.

claims.evidence: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults named consequences.
Daily supplement in winter for everyone; higher-risk groups all year.

additions.sentence: The routine test measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D because it is the best marker of overall vitamin D status and stays in the blood longer than the active form.
additions.evidence: Test measures 25(OH)D; best marker of overall status; stays longer at higher concentrations than active form.

additions.sentence: The liver makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D first, and the kidneys then convert it into the fully active form.
additions.evidence: Liver makes 25(OH)D, kidneys convert it to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

additions.sentence: Children under five are advised to take vitamin drops containing vitamin D all year.
additions.evidence: Children under 5 advised to take vitamin drops year-round (Scottish Government guidance).

additions.sentence: People aged 65 and over, and those who are housebound or live in care homes, are also considered at higher risk.
additions.evidence: NHS inform names housebound, indoors, care home residents; another NHS source adds age 65 and over.

additions.sentence: One NHS formulary says re-testing is generally left until at least three months after treatment starts.
additions.evidence: A minimum of three months after starting treatment is advisable before re-testing.

additions.sentence: One NHS policy says the evidence linking low vitamin D to conditions other than bone health is inconsistent or absent.
additions.evidence: Evidence linking low vitamin D to non-bone conditions is either inconsistent or absent.

notes: nhs.uk vitamin D page was listed but its text was not returned, so NHS England attributions were reworded to UK public health or local NHS guidance. NHS inform says supplement for over-ones; Scottish Government says from age five; c19 follows the Scottish Government.
